title: Trace delegate invocation and captured variables, including the bound target and multicast order, return value and failure behavior

rubric.point: Both lambdas capture the same variable `total`, meaning shared storage, rather than each getting its own copy or a snapshot of its value at creation.
`read` gets the variable's current value when it is invoked. By then, the two `add()` calls have written 10 to that same storage.

questions.model: Both lambdas close over the same variable `total`, so they share its storage. Neither stores a copy of its value. Each `add()` call updates that storage, so `total` becomes 10. `read()` reads the current value when it is called, which is 10.

options: `A` then `B`: the method-group delegate stored object A as its target when it was created, while the lambda captured the variable `a` and reads it at call time.
`A` then `A`: both delegates stored a snapshot of `a` when they were created, so reassigning the local afterwards cannot affect either of them.
`B` then `B`: both delegates read the variable `a` when invoked, because a delegate stores only the method and never the object to call it on.
`B` then `A`: the method-group delegate reads `a` at call time, while the lambda copied the value of `a` into itself when it was created.

rubric.point: Chooses `A` then `B`, because the closed instance delegate binds its target object at creation and the lambda captures the variable, which it reads when invoked.

questions.model: `A` then `B`. `a.Report` creates a closed instance delegate whose target is the object `a` referred to at that moment: Counter A. Reassigning `a` later does not change the delegate's stored target. The lambda captures the variable `a` itself, so when it runs it reads the current value, Counter B.

annotations.note: You correctly say `read` evaluates `total` when it is invoked, not when it was created.
This doesn't explain why the invocation returns 10. You needed to say that the `add()` calls wrote to the same storage that `read` then reads.
You didn't say that both lambdas capture the same variable `total`, so they share storage. A lambda that closes over a variable holds a reference to that variable, so 'not state' is misleading.
